summary: This document defines the TLS Certificate Status Version 2 extension, which lets clients support several certificate status methods; the use of Certificate Status is commonly called OCSP stapling. It also defines an OCSP-based method that lets servers give status for intermediate certificates in the chain, not just their own. It was later replaced by RFC 8446 and RFC 9846.

plainLanguage.summary: A website brings a fresh "still valid" note for its ID and for the helpers who vouched for it. This was later replaced by newer rules.

subtitle: Bringing fresh certificate status checks into the TLS handshake.

tldr.problem: The original Certificate Status extension (OCSP stapling) allows a TLS server to send the status of its own certificate during the handshake, reducing client verification delays. However, it cannot provide status for intermediate CA certificates, and clients cannot indicate support for multiple certificate status methods.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the status_request_v2 extension, which allows clients to request multiple certificate status methods in a single list, and introduces ocsp_multi mode so servers can provide OCSP responses for the entire certificate chain, not just the end-entity certificate.
tldr.outcome: Clients can now verify the entire certificate chain during a single TLS handshake, eliminating the need for separate validation requests to CRLs or OCSP servers for intermediate certificates.

facts.label: Response list can be incomplete
facts.value: Yes, fewer responses than certificates is allowed

today: RFC 6961 was updated by RFC 8446 and RFC 9846. Modern TLS implementations now widely support OCSP stapling and multi-certificate status extensions, making certificate chain verification faster and more privacy-preserving.

sections.title: OCSP Stapling Basics
sections.content:
OCSP stapling refers to the TLS Certificate Status extension defined in RFC 6066. During a TLS handshake, a client can request that the server provide the current revocation status of its certificate using the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP). The server sends a signed OCSP response along with its certificate, eliminating the need for the client to make a separate request to the certificate authority's OCSP server.

This reduces handshake time and network delays, and lowers the load on the certificate issuer's OCSP servers. However, the original extension has two key limitations: it only provides status for the server's certificate, not for intermediate CA certificates, and clients cannot indicate support for multiple status request methods.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking a government office separately if a certificate is still good, the website just brings a recent official letter proving it is good. Much faster.

sections.title: The Problem with Version 1
sections.content:
Modern TLS uses a certificate chain: the server's end-entity certificate is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA. When a client validates the chain, it must verify that all certificates, including intermediate CAs, are not revoked. The original Certificate Status extension only allows the client to request status for the end-entity certificate.

If an intermediate CA is revoked, clients must verify it separately, typically using Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) or by directly querying the OCSP server. This introduces additional requests, delays, and privacy concerns (the OCSP server learns which sites are being visited). Furthermore, the original extension format does not allow clients to express support for newer or alternative status methods without creating incompatibilities with older servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The old system only brought a note for the main ID, not for the helpers. If a helper ID was bad, you had to ask separately and wait.

sections.title: The status_request_v2 Extension
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new TLS extension called status_request_v2 (extension type 17). Clients send this extension in their ClientHello to indicate support for one or more certificate status methods. The extension contains a list of CertificateStatusRequestItemV2 records, each specifying a status method type and any parameters for that method.

Two status types are defined: ocsp (value 1), which is the original single-certificate OCSP request, and ocsp_multi (value 2), which requests OCSP responses for multiple certificates in the chain. The client lists these in order of preference. A server receiving this extension MAY choose to return a CertificateStatus message using one of the requested methods, or it MAY choose not to respond with status information.
sections.plainLanguage: The new extension is like a preferences list: the client says "I can handle status in these ways, in this order." The server picks one or just ignores the list.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
When a client sends status_request_v2, it may include parameters in the OCSPStatusRequest structure: a list of responder IDs (OCSP responders the client trusts) and OCSP request extensions (such as a nonce for replay protection). The server SHOULD use this information when selecting an OCSP responder and forming its OCSP request.

For ocsp_multi mode, the server sends an OCSPResponseList containing one OCSP response per certificate in the chain, in the same order. The response list may contain fewer responses than certificates if the server does not have cached responses for all of them; individual response entries may be empty (zero bytes) if no response is available. If the client receives an incomplete response list, it SHOULD validate missing certificates through alternative methods such as CRLs. The client MUST check each OCSP response for revocation status and abort the handshake if a certificate is found to be revoked.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can say which people it trusts to check the IDs, and ask for special security tricks. The server brings OCSP notes for each ID in the chain, or admits it does not have some of them.

sections.title: Security and Status Handling
sections.content:
A client that requires OCSP validation MUST understand that an attacker might use a compromised key to pretend that OCSP stapling is not supported. Such a client should either contact the OCSP server directly or abort the handshake. The RFC clarifies the encoding of OCSP nonce extensions for improved replay attack protection.

OCSP responses can be inconclusive: they may neither confirm "good" status nor report "revoked" status. In such cases, the TLS client may attempt to validate the certificate through other means. If no definite status is obtained, the client MUST abort the connection unless the application explicitly allows it to proceed (for example, in EAP-TLS scenarios where other mechanisms can validate the certificate later). The client MUST NOT disclose sensitive information until it has fully validated the server certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor might pretend the feature does not exist. If you really need the check, you should ask separately. Also, sometimes the answer is "I do not know," and you have to decide if that is good enough.
